This study examines four higher education projects (HEPs) established in exile by Russian emigrants following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine and subsequent state repression of academia, including censorship, "foreign agent" labelling, and politically motivated layoffs that forced thousands of scholars to leave. Drawing on phenomenological interviews with project leaders and discourse analysis of self-presentation materials, the paper explores how relocated HEPs conceptualise themselves in relation to their homeland and what goals they present to broader society. The study frames HEPs within "education in emergencies" and the concept of "exiled consciousness"—an anticipation of eventual return that shapes exiles' strategies. Findings reveal three narratives of self-conceptualisation: first, HEPs act as "safe havens," providing infrastructure, teaching positions, and spaces of intellectual freedom for fleeing scholars and students; second, they preserve their academic heritage, including schools of thought and the Russian academic language, though reconceptualisation of this heritage remains limited; third, they engage in "hope-making praxis," transforming anticipation of return into active, pragmatic work toward a desired future for Russia, regardless of whether return occurs. The paper concludes that HEPs serve as sanctuaries, safeguard academic legacies, and foster social transformation through hope-fuelled praxis, while identifying directions for further research, including long-term study of HEPs' evolving self-conceptualisation and their role in reshaping international education.

Players said they approached the game as a single game and gained confidence from the result, despite having seen Dominik Hasek only once during the season. They credited the forwards' back pressure and effort for helping the defensemen and goaltender against Detroit's speed. They expect a strong effort from a perennial all-star team and do not know what changes the opponent may make. Their style is straightforward: four lines and six defensemen playing the same way, with a goaltender expected to make saves. One player, whose hometown is Detroit, said he has avoided off-ice distractions to stay focused. The team emphasized keeping games close throughout the playoff series against New Jersey, Montreal, and Toronto, since falling behind Detroit forces them to open up. Ron Francis was described as a classy, laissez-faire captain whom the team plays for, and young players' inexperience has helped them handle pressure. Players said perfection is impossible against Detroit's fast, big team, that hitting was evenly matched, and that Detroit will likely regroup with the same effort. They stressed not changing their approach, possibly taking shorter shifts, and acknowledged early-game nerves that eased as the game progressed.

This passage presents a cost-effectiveness analysis of nutritional supplementation for tuberculosis (TB) prevention in India. TB is the leading infectious cause of death worldwide (10.6 million cases, 1.3 million deaths in 2022), and undernutrition is its leading risk factor, associated with higher death, treatment failure, and relapse risks among TB patients. The RATIONS trial in eastern India randomized over 10,000 household contacts of persons with TB (PWTB) to routine care or a food basket costing $13 monthly for 6 months, finding a 40% reduction in TB incidence and approximately 35% lower mortality among PWTB receiving nutritional support.

The authors developed a Markov state transition model simulating 100,000 HIV-negative household contacts over their lifetime, conducted from Indian government and societal perspectives. The intervention assumed an incidence rate ratio of 0.61 for two years and a mortality risk ratio of 0.65.

Base case results showed reduced lifetime TB incidence (6,749 vs. 7,718 cases per 100,000), reduced TB deaths (906 vs. 1,529), and 13,775 DALYs averted. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was $229 per DALY averted (healthcare perspective) and $184 (societal perspective), both below India's willingness-to-pay threshold of $550. Results were most sensitive to supplementation costs and the TB incidence risk ratio; the intervention remained cost-effective at supplementation costs below $75. Probabilistic analyses favored the intervention in over 99% of simulations. The authors conclude that RATIONS-style nutritional support would be cost-effective for reducing TB incidence and mortality in India, while noting limitations such as unmodeled transmission reductions, relapses, and drug-resistant TB costs.

Martin Brodeur said his team is enjoying its playoff run and, while still alive in the finals, aims for more success and will not give up. He stressed creating offensive zone space by driving players to the net, noted the adjustment to a western conference opponent, and said the team must build on its recent late third-period win, as the opponent stands one win from its dream. He mentioned relaxing on his son's birthday, said pressure has decreased with age, and noted home games make focusing easier.

The speaker finds the video of a goal inconclusive but says the team must trust Toronto and the referees. He attributes the goals to tough bounces, says Pekks has been the best playoff performer, and praises Milwaukee's organization, which helped him mature on and off the ice.

A newborn girl from a faith-healing church family died shortly after birth at an Oregon City home from complications of prematurity; the medical examiner said immediate care could have saved her. Her twin survived. No charges have been filed; deputies are investigating.

The lecture introduces dynamic optimality: the open question of whether there exists a single binary search tree (BST) that is at least as good as all others. It defines the BST model of computation, where keys are stored in a BST and allowed operations are following left, right, and parent pointers in constant time and rotating a node with its parent. Searches start at the root and must visit the target key; only successful searches are considered, with no insertions or deletions. Although log n per access is necessary in the worst case, the goal is to perform well on every access sequence.

Several properties are presented: the sequential access property (accessing keys in order costs constant amortized time), the dynamic finger property (cost log k when consecutive accesses are k apart in key space), the entropy property (cost based on access frequencies), the working set property (cost log of the number of distinct keys accessed since the current key's last access), and the unified property (2001), which pays the log of the sum of spatial and temporal distances to a recently accessed nearby key. No known BST achieves the unified property; the best achieves it plus log log n.

Dynamic optimality requires an online BST whose total cost is within a constant factor of the offline optimal BST algorithm; this is open, though log log n competitiveness is known. Splay trees are conjectured to be dynamically optimal; they satisfy the sequential access, working set, entropy, and dynamic finger properties, but dynamic optimality remains unproven.

The lecture then presents a geometric view (from an MIT PhD thesis with collaborators, published 2009): an access sequence maps to points (space versus time), and a BST algorithm maps to the nodes touched. A point set is a valid BST execution if and only if it is arborally satisfied—every rectangle spanned by two points not on a common horizontal or vertical line contains another point. Dynamic optimality thus becomes finding the minimum number of points to add to satisfy the access point set; the best known approximation is log log n. The proof uses lowest common ancestors in one direction and treaps heap-ordered by next access time in the other.

Finally, the greedy algorithm—adding points row by row to satisfy rectangles—is conjectured offline optimal. Originally considered offline (1988 thesis, rediscovered 2000), the geometric view enables an online implementation using split trees. Lower bounds, discussed next class, almost prove greedy optimal.

The lecture examines finite-temperature CFTs on the sphere and their gravity duals. Unlike a CFT on flat space, where temperature is the only scale so physics is identical at all temperatures, a CFT on a sphere has a dimensionless parameter rT, making physics temperature-dependent.

In global AdS, both thermal AdS (a thermal gas) and black hole solutions exist. Unlike the flat-space case, thermal AdS is allowed on the sphere because the Euclidean metric remains non-singular—the thermal circle's proper length is bounded below by beta. The black hole solution's Hawking temperature, as a function of horizon radius r0, has a maximum beta, implying a minimum temperature T_min. Above T_min, two black hole solutions exist: a "big" black hole with positive specific heat and a "small" black hole with negative specific heat, which behaves like a flat-space Schwarzschild black hole when much smaller than the AdS curvature radius.

With three saddle points at a given temperature, the dominant phase is the one with lowest free energy. This follows both from thermodynamics and from the saddle-point approximation, since each Euclidean action scales as N squared, so the largest exponential dominates at large N. The small black hole never dominates. There exists a critical temperature Tc (greater than T_min): below T_min only thermal AdS exists; between T_min and Tc thermal AdS dominates; above Tc the big black hole dominates. This is the Hawking-Page transition—a first-order phase transition where the free energy is continuous but its first derivative, of order N squared, is discontinuous. The transition occurs when the black hole size equals the AdS radius. The transition was discovered in 1981, before the AdS/CFT conjecture.

The field theory interpretation is illustrated with a toy model of 2N squared free harmonic oscillators arranged into matrices A and B, subject to an SU(N) singlet (trace) condition. States with energy of order 1 have density of states of order N^0, while states with energy of order N squared have density of states exponential in N squared. At low temperature (large beta), thermal suppression prevents high-energy states from contributing to the free energy; at sufficiently high temperature, the entropy overwhelms the suppression and order N squared states dominate, reproducing the Hawking-Page transition. The phenomenon depends only on large N and the density of states, not on system details.

Faviola Dadis accused Steven Seagal of sexually assaulting her during a 2002 casting session at a Beverly Hills hotel when she was 17. Speaking at a Los Angeles news conference, she described the assault and its lasting effects, including depression, anxiety, and PTSD. She recently filed a police report, and prosecutors are reviewing the case. Dadis said she was inspired to come forward by other accusers, including Regina Simons and Jenny McCarthy. Seagal has denied the allegations, and no lawsuits are planned.

The top-seeded Bemidji Blue Ox won the Region 10C tournament title by defeating Crookston in Saturday's championship. Crookston had earlier clinched a state berth by beating Moorhead 3-2 in extra innings. Ben Thoma earned the win with seven innings pitched, seven strikeouts and one run allowed, while Cody Benson went 3-for-5 at the plate. As region champion, the Blue Ox receive a first-round bye in the 48-team state tournament hosted by Green Isle, Hamburg and Norwood Young America. Bemidji opens play Aug. 27 against the Fort Ripley/Blue Earth winner.

Dale Capstick of Coxheath, Cape Breton, has seen about three dozen large spiders in her home since August, and her husband has killed about 30. A specimen caught by Charles Andrews was confirmed by biologist Calum Ewing of the Nova Scotia Museum as Eratigena atrica, the giant house spider. Native to western Europe, the spiders first appeared in Nova Scotia in the mid-1990s. Ewing said they are harmless, with bodies 10 to 18 millimetres long and leg spans up to 10 centimetres. Known as "bathtub spiders," they are attracted by insect prey and die or leave once the prey is gone.

Meizu has cut prices of its Pro 7 and Pro 7 Plus smartphones in China, with the series now starting at 1,999 Yuan from 12th December. The Pro 7 has a 5.2-inch Super AMOLED display with a secondary screen, while the Pro 7 Plus has a 5.7-inch display. Both feature dual 12-megapixel Sony IMX386 rear cameras, a 16-megapixel front camera, and run Flyme OS 6 based on Android Nougat.

Rushin Shah, Apple's former head of Natural Language Understanding for Siri, has left the company after five years to join Facebook's Menlo Park headquarters. Shah helped build key Siri features, including voice recognition and the ability to interpret user intent from natural speech. At Facebook, he will work on natural language and dialogue understanding, possibly developing a rival to Siri or extending the "M" assistant. His departure comes as Siri faces competition from Amazon's Alexa and Google Assistant.

The latest Canadian Couch Potato podcast explores the trade-off between cost and complexity in investing, featuring John Robertson, author of The Value of Simple (second edition). Robertson discusses indexing options, robo-advisors, his AutoInvest.ca comparison tool, and his online course Practical Index Investing for Canadians. The Ask the Spud segment examines Vanguard's new asset allocation ETFs (VBAL, VGRO, VCNS), which carry a 0.22% fee but may not suit everyone. Before switching from Tangerine or TD e-Series funds, investors should consider portfolio size, automation of contributions (unavailable with ETFs), trading experience, account complexity, and target asset mix—only 60% or 80% equity options exist, and conservative investors may prefer GICs.

ESA has inaugurated a new 35-meter deep space antenna, "New Norcia 3," at its New Norcia station in Western Australia, about 115 km north of Perth. It is the fourth antenna in ESA's Estrack deep space tracking network and the second at the site, which will become ESA's first ground station with two deep space antennas. Construction began in 2021, cost EUR 62.3 million (including a EUR 3 million contribution from the Australian Space Agency), and was led by co-prime contractors Thales Alenia Space and Schwartz Hautmont, with several Australian companies involved. The antenna features components cryogenically cooled to around -263°C to detect weak signals and a 20kW amplifier for transmitting commands to distant spacecraft. Entering service in 2026, it will support missions including Juice, Solar Orbiter, BepiColombo, Mars Express, and Hera, plus upcoming missions such as Plato, Envision, Ariel, Ramses, and Vigil. It can also support other agencies including NASA, JAXA, and ISRO. The station is operated locally by CSIRO and is expected to generate economic value and employment over a projected 50-year lifetime.

Researchers led by UCL and Imperial College London have shown for the first time how polymyxins, last-resort antibiotics against Gram-negative bacteria, kill bacterial cells. Using high-resolution imaging and biochemical experiments, the team found that Polymyxin B rapidly causes bumps and bulges on the bacterial surface, triggering the cell to overproduce and shed its outer armor. This leaves gaps in the cell's defenses, allowing the antibiotic to enter and kill it. However, this process only occurs in active bacteria; dormant cells, which switch off armor production, are unaffected and can later reawaken to cause recurrent infections. When dormant cells were given sugar, the antibiotic killed them after a 15-minute delay needed to resume armor production. The findings could inspire strategies such as combining polymyxins with treatments that wake dormant bacteria or promote armor production.

At its Discover 2017 conference on June 6, HPE unveiled the Edgeline Services Platform and two apps—the Data Aggregation App and the Address Translation App—to help customers manage growing IoT device inventories and combine IT and OT functions. Called Software Defined OT, the offerings build on HPE's Edgeline Converged Edge systems and run IoT applications where equipment is located. The Data Aggregation App combines data from OT devices like PLCs and SCADA systems, while the Address Translation App delivers network address translations to subset networks and can be managed remotely. Analyst Mike Krell said HPE's single-vendor approach offers value in a crowded market.

The Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia answered certified questions from the Circuit Court of Mercer County concerning three at-will cleaning maids—Deborah Cordle, Brenda Billings, and Brenda Hall—who were terminated by General Hugh Mercer Corporation, operator of a Holiday Inn in Princeton, after refusing to take polygraph tests. The plaintiffs had signed a 1981 agreement consenting to such testing, refused when testing was announced in 1982, and were fired in October 1982. The circuit court denied the defendant's motion to dismiss and certified whether the termination violated a substantial public policy of West Virginia and whether determining public policy is a question of law or fact.

The majority held that determining public policy is a question of law for the court, not the jury. It further held that at-will employees are protected from discharges contravening substantial public policy, citing Harless v. First National Bank. Relying on West Virginia privacy precedents (Sutherland, Roach, and Golden) and treating the subsequently enacted statute limiting employer polygraph use as embodying a recognized public policy, the court held it contrary to West Virginia public policy for an employer to require a polygraph test as a condition of employment, affirmed the circuit court, and remanded for further proceedings.

Justice Miller dissented, arguing no established public policy prohibited such discharges when the plaintiffs were fired, since the 1983 statute took effect approximately nine months after termination, and that the cited privacy cases were inapplicable. Justice Neely also dissented, contending the ruling had an unfair retroactive effect and that the legislature had adequately addressed the issue prospectively.

The speaker said the opposing goalie played well in a goaltending duel and the opponent won. The series is now a three-game series for the Stanley Cup against Tampa Bay. He stressed the need for a killer instinct, better scoring chances, and burying shots, while dismissing concerns about officiating.

The passage, from the SD Physical Layer Simplified Specification Version 6.00, describes card initialization, identification, and data transfer procedures.

After bus activation, the host starts initialization with ACMD41, setting operational conditions and the HCS bit in the OCR (HCS=1 indicates SDHC/SDXC support). Cards that did not respond to CMD8 ignore HCS, and the host should set HCS=0 in that case. The OCR busy bit signals initialization completion, which must occur within 1 second of the first ACMD41; while repeating ACMD41, the host may issue only CMD0. The CCS field in the response indicates card type (CCS=0: SDSC; CCS=1: SDHC/SDXC). The host then issues CMD2 to obtain each card's CID and CMD3 to obtain a relative card address (RCA), after which the card enters Stand-by State. SDXC initialization is identical to SDHC, with user area capacity of at least 32GB.

For UHS-I, the host sets S18R=1 to request 1.8V signaling; if the card responds with S18A=1, the host issues CMD11 to perform voltage switch, with completion checked via DAT[3:0]. Sampling point tuning uses repeated CMD19 executions (up to 40 within 150ms).

In Data Transfer Mode, the host uses CMD9 to obtain the CSD, optional CMD4 (SET_DSR) to configure driver stages, and CMD7 to select one card into Transfer State (RCA 0x0000 deselects all cards). Read commands (CMD17, CMD18, CMD30, ACMD51, CMD56) and write commands (CMD24, CMD25, CMD27, CMD42, CMD56) can be aborted with CMD12. The card buffers block writes and holds DAT0 low while busy; parameter set and read commands are not allowed during programming. Bus width is changed via ACMD6 (default 1-bit; rejected when locked).

Block reads (CMD17 single, CMD18 multiple) use blocks up to 512 bytes with CRC. Block writes require 512-byte block length on SDHC/SDXC; ACMD23 sets a pre-erase count to speed multiple block writes, and ACMD22 reports the number of well-written blocks. Erase uses CMD32/CMD33 address setting followed by CMD38; DISCARD (argument 00000001h) and FULE (full user area logical erase, argument 00000002h) variants are supported only for SDHC/SDXC and not via SPI, with busy timeouts of 250ms and 1 second respectively.

Write protection comprises a mechanical switch (host responsibility), optional internal protection, and password lock/unlock via CMD42 using non-volatile PWD/PWD_LEN registers. Locked cards execute only class 0 commands, ACMD41, CMD16, and lock-class commands. Card Ownership Protection (COP, Version 5.10+) adds FEP (Force Erase Password) registers; when FEP is set, Force Erase and Clear PWD are disabled and COP Unlock (CMD42[1Fh]) is required after power-on or reset.

APP_CMD (CMD55) causes the following command to be interpreted as an application-specific command. CMD6 (Switch Function) supports function groups for access mode, command system, driver strength, and power limit, with Mode 0 (check) and Mode 1 (set) operations returning 512 bits of status; the default Power Limit is 0.72W. High-Speed mode (25 MB/sec at 50 MHz) is selected via CMD6 and requires one card per host. CMD8 verifies host supply voltage and expands ACMD41 functionality. SDHC/SDXC use block addressing with fixed 512-byte blocks and disable partial, misaligned, and write-protected-group access, while SDSC uses byte addressing with CMD16-defined block lengths.

Austin police chief Brian Manley appealed to whoever carried out three package bombings that killed two people—Draylen Mason, 17, and Anthony Stephan House, 39—and injured two others, urging them to contact authorities. All victims were black or Hispanic, and a hate crime has not been ruled out. The reward was increased to $100,000, plus Gov. Abbott's $15,000. Some 500 federal agents are assisting, with 735 suspicious packages reported, 236 interviews logged, and 435 leads checked.

UK Chancellor Rachel Reeves has declined to rule out tax increases ahead of November's budget, citing geopolitical instability, new U.S. tariffs, and rising borrowing costs as factors that have changed the economic landscape since Labour's manifesto was published. While commitments such as avoiding VAT increases remain policy for now, she and Chief Secretary Darren Jones would not explicitly rule out breaking manifesto tax caps. With forecasts pointing to a fiscal shortfall of up to £30 billion, analysts suggest Reeves is deliberately keeping her options open, balancing market credibility and fiscal discipline against voter expectations, leaving businesses and households uncertain about potential policy changes.

Bishop Hassan Kukah of the Catholic Diocese of Sokoto urged Nigerian politicians to provide quality governance and commended the military for its patience in allowing democracy to evolve, saying the frustrations of the past 17 years would have triggered several coups if such takeovers were still in vogue. Speaking at the Kukah Centre in Abuja, he condemned religious sentiment used to cover misgovernance, said Nigerians share blame for bad governance for failing to question leaders' promises, and cautioned politicians against taking the military's patience for granted. He urged government tolerance of opposing views and announced a leadership forum, with Ghanaian President Nana Akufo Addo to deliver a lecture on sustaining democracy in Africa.

Microsoft Corporation filed a Form 8-K with the SEC dated January 29, 2020, announcing financial results for the fiscal quarter ended December 31, 2019, via a press release furnished as Exhibit 99.1. The filing lists Microsoft's registered securities: common stock ($0.00000625 par value) and 2.125% Notes due 2021, 3.125% Notes due 2028, and 2.625% Notes due 2033, all trading on NASDAQ under the symbol MSFT. This email compiles news articles from May 9, 2001 concerning Enron. Questia Media, an online college library and research firm backed by investors including Enron Chairman Ken Lay, laid off 139 employees—nearly half its workforce—citing difficulty raising additional funds, though paying subscribers had reportedly grown fivefold in two weeks. Market reports noted the Dow fell 51.66 points to 10,883.51 while the Nasdaq rose 25.20 to 2,198.77; Enron shares fell $1.93 to $56.11. In Japan, Enron officials said the newly deregulated power market lacked real competition, with newcomers holding only 0.2 percent of the market, and called for an independent regulator, citing concerns about METI's relationship with incumbent utilities. Separately, U.S. energy company Williams announced it would enter Europe's deregulating gas and power markets with a London-based trading operation. Multiple articles covered Enron's troubled Dabhol Power Company project in India: families of expatriate executives were relocated to Singapore and security was tightened amid uncertainty over the project's fate; MSEB denied underutilizing its own capacity to justify purchases from Dabhol and said it faced no federal pressure to maintain the agreement; MSEB appointed former Bombay High Court judge M.L. Pendse as arbitrator, with proceedings to occur in London; the Swadeshi Jagran Manch demanded a judicial probe into the Enron deal; MSEB stated increased generation from its Uran plant was unviable due to fuel costs; and lenders to the project said they would back termination of the power purchase agreement, with the deadline set for May 15. The passage is from the datasheet of the ADS8681W, ADS8685W, and ADS8689W, 16-bit SAR ADC data acquisition devices from Texas Instruments.

- **ADC Transfer Function:** The device supports single-ended and differential inputs with bipolar and unipolar ranges, outputting data in straight-binary format. LSB size equals FSR/2¹⁶.
- **Alarm Features:** Two alarm types are provided—an input alarm with user-programmable high/low thresholds and hysteresis, and an AVDD alarm with fixed trip points (4.7V low, 5.3V high). Active and tripped alarm flags are readable via the ALARM pin, the ALARM_REG register, or appended to the data output.
- **Digital Interface:** The multiSPI interface supports legacy SPI-compatible protocols (single or dual SDO) and source-synchronous (SRC) protocols for data reads. Connection topologies include single-device and daisy-chain configurations, with daisy-chain frames requiring 32 × N SCLK edges.
- **Operational Modes:** The device has three states—RESET (application reset or power-on reset), ACQ, and CONV—controlled by the RST and CONVST/CS signals.
- **Programming:** Data transfer frames are 32 bits; nine configuration registers cover device ID, reset/power control, SPI settings, data output control, range selection, alarms, and alarm thresholds.
- **Applications:** An example design combines the ADS8681W with the MUX36D08 multiplexer for an eight-channel industrial analog input module supporting standard voltage and current ranges (e.g., ±10V, 4–20mA) for PLCs, DCS, and DAS systems.
- **Power Recommendations:** Separate AVDD and DVDD supplies require decoupling capacitors; NAP and power-down modes reduce consumption at lower throughput rates. PCB layout guidelines address analog/digital partitioning and reference capacitor placement.
- **Revision History:** Revision A (May 2025) changed ADS8685W and ADS8689W status from Advance Information to Production Data.

In this 1952 California appeal, a mother challenged a judgment awarding custody of her son Edward to the father. After the mother moved to Nevada in 1946 and obtained a divorce, the father had custody of Edward from age 2, except for a 14-month period beginning in 1949 when the mother retained him after a visit. The mother argued that under Civil Code section 138, a child of tender years should be given to the mother when the parents are equally fit. The court held that the child's best interests—including his established home life with the father—justified the custody award, and affirmed the judgment.

This MIT OpenCourseWare lecture introduces ordinary differential equation initial value problems (ODE-IVPs). The instructor explains how to convert higher-order ODEs into first-order standard form for Matlab solvers, which expect f(t,y). The Forward Euler method is derived from a Taylor expansion and likened to the rectangle rule, which carries a total error of order delta t. Higher-order update formulas, such as the trapezoid and midpoint rules, reduce the error to order delta t squared; Runge-Kutta methods extend this further, with Matlab's ode45 using fourth- and fifth-order extensions, comparing them to estimate error and adjust step size. Because f depends on the unknown y rather than a known t, midpoint estimates require approximations such as Forward Euler predictions. Error propagation across repeated extrapolation steps is analyzed through the matrix (identity plus delta t times the Jacobian); numerical stability requires its norm to be no greater than 1. Equations with positive Jacobian eigenvalues are inherently unstable, but even stable equations can produce oscillating, exploding numerical solutions if the step size is too large, as demonstrated with dy/dt = -2y solved by Forward Euler. Homework 4 requires writing an ODE solver, and implicit solvers will be covered in the next lecture.

This chapter addresses modeling and validation of digital business processes in the extended enterprise (EE) context, where organizations share common goals and processes span company boundaries. Relying on OMG's Model Driven Architecture, the authors define a business process model comprising three components: a static domain model (domain entities), a workflow model (process activities), and a value model (value exchange between parties).

Business rules (BR) are expressed via controlled natural languages such as Attempto Controlled English (ACE) and SBVR, which can be translated into logic-based formulations (e.g., Discourse Representation Structures, OWL DL, RuleML). Automated reasoning over BR requires hybrid deduction combining open-world assumption (OWA) reasoning, suited to incomplete, heterogeneous knowledge, with closed-world assumption (CWA) reasoning, suited to data under full stakeholder control. Some business rules cannot be expressed in OWL DL or Horn rules alone, such as certain existential constraints or constraints on n-ary relations. Interpretation issues arise when integrating OWL's model-theoretic approach with SWRL's single-model approach. Business rules also carry modalities: alethic rules express necessities that cannot be violated, while deontic rules express obligations that may be violated; tools such as Halpin's NORMA support both, but selecting an appropriate modal logic poses tractability challenges.

Process flows are typically described with graphical notations such as BPMN and UML Activity Diagrams, with formalizations including Petri nets, pi-calculus, situation calculus, and temporal logic. Model checking faces state space explosion; symbolic encoding via temporal logics (LTL, CTL) and strong fairness constraints offers a mitigation. Declarative representations support consistency checking, data exportation, and annotation.

Value models estimate profitability for each stakeholder in a collaboration. Both graphical (e3-value) and logic-based (Prolog-style FOL) representations explicitly model actors and value exchanges, enabling profitability calculations for decision making.

Relations among models are organized across business rules, business, process, and implementation layers. Consistency relations include static consistency (exchanged values correspond to exchanged business objects), semi-dynamic consistency (value model forecasts achievable by the process flow), and dynamic consistency (execution consistent with expected behavior, evaluated via log files through monitoring consistency). Process mining can derive process models from log data.

The conclusion states that business process models require multi-faceted representation supporting a priori feasibility evaluation and evolution based on run-time evidence, with different facets requiring different formalisms integrated through hybrid reasoning. Open issues include critical areas detection and representing pragmatics, such as stakeholders' reasons for actions and the customer perspective.

Casino mogul Steve Wynn brokered a 2006 settlement with a second woman accusing him of sexual misconduct, according to court documents from his attorneys. Wynn recently met with FBI agents to accuse the woman, a former Wynn employee, of extortion for threatening to publicize the settlement's details. Her attorney, Lisa Bloom, denied the extortion claims, saying her client's emails sought no money. Wynn resigned as Wynn Resorts' chairman and CEO after the Wall Street Journal reported several women accused him of harassment or assault, including a $7.5 million settlement with a former manicurist. Wynn denies the accusations, attributing them to his ex-wife's campaign, which her attorney denies. The settlements surfaced during a civil case scheduled for trial in April.

This article presents a qualitative document analysis examining digital storytelling (DST) in African higher education and teacher training, guided by two research questions: what skills DST promotes in African education, and in what contexts it is integrated into African higher education.

The literature review defines DST as the art of storytelling using digital tools such as text, graphics, sound, and video, typically consisting of short narratives with seven essential elements. The creation process involves pre-production, production, and post-production phases. Identified benefits include improved digital and media literacy, motivation, engagement, critical thinking, problem-solving, writing skills, creativity, and learning autonomy. DST is interdisciplinary and has shown effectiveness across subjects including science, mathematics, psychology, and social studies. In Africa, where storytelling has traditionally served as a medium for transmitting history and values, DST serves both educational and cultural purposes, including preserving indigenous knowledge and languages.

The methodology involved analyzing 15 scientific articles (filtered from 35 using a PRISMA protocol-based checklist) from databases including Google Scholar, ERIC, JSTOR, and ResearchGate, covering African studies from 2000 to the present. Studies were conducted in South Africa, Nigeria, Egypt, Tanzania, Uganda, and Kenya, with most adopting qualitative approaches.

Results indicate DST promotes empowerment through identity expression, cultural enrichment, and transformative learning experiences. Specific findings include increased student engagement, community building among diverse pre-service teachers, improved oral performance, enhanced map-reading skills in geography, development of higher-order thinking and reflective capabilities, and support for social activism among marginalized groups. However, challenges persist, including resource shortages, lack of self-confidence, rigid curricula, inconsistent electricity, insufficient digital equipment, and limited technological proficiency.

The conclusion states that DST functions not merely as a technological tool but as a transformative force in African higher education, demonstrating adaptability across various academic settings and providing a foundation for future research and educational innovation.

Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, who lives in Islington and has frequently spoken against air pollution, uses a chauffeur-driven Ford Galaxy diesel that waited 40 minutes on double yellow lines outside his home before travelling six miles to Westminster. The car emits 189g of CO2, sits in the fourth-highest tax band, and will incur Sadiq Khan's Ultra Low Emission Zone charge from April 2019. Tory MP Andrew Bridgen accused Corbyn of "breathtaking hypocrisy", noting Islington and Hackney councils have proposed banning diesel cars with £130 fines. Corbyn, who does not own a car and was previously a keen cyclist, accepted the Government Car Service perk in 2015 after being advised to stop cycling for security reasons, despite living less than half a mile from a Tube station. A traffic warden did not ticket the parked car.

Brazil's CPFL Energia SA launched Envo, a new firm targeting the growing market for solar-powered homes. Envo will offer equipment, installation, and assistance connecting systems to the power grid. CEO Andre Dorf cited rising consumer environmental concerns and growing solar grid connections. Banco Santander Brasil will offer financing for Envo clients.

This is the introductory lecture of MIT's graduate course 8.422, the second part of a two-course sequence on atomic, molecular, and optical (AMO) physics. The professor defines AMO physics as what AMO researchers do, built from atoms, molecules, photons, and electromagnetic fields, and characterizes it as low-energy quantum physics. The field has evolved from studying individual gas-phase particles and collisions toward few-body and many-body physics, overlapping with quantum information science and condensed matter physics.

The professor traces the field's progression from observing nature to controlling it: control of internal states via optical pumping (Nobel Prize to Kastler, 1966), control of motion through laser cooling and Bose-Einstein condensation, and control of single quantum systems (recently recognized with a Nobel Prize). Technological advances drove this evolution, including affordable solid-state lasers, ultrashort high-intensity pulses, frequency combs (Nobel Prize 2005), and high-finesse cavities enabling single-photon physics. Paradigmatic topics have shifted from atomic structure and laser spectroscopy to laser cooling, Bose-Einstein condensation, ultracold fermions, and entanglement.

Regarding logistics: prerequisites are 8.05 and 8.06 (perturbation theory); assessment consists of ten problem sets and a term paper, with no exams; the course meets Monday/Wednesday with occasional Friday makeup sessions; five TAs from active MIT research groups support the course. Topics include QED and light-atom interactions from first principles, open systems and master equations, mechanical forces of light, trapping and cooling, single photons, quantum information building blocks, and many-body physics of quantum gases. Excluded are high-energy physics, advanced atomic structure, and high-intensity lasers.

As an appetizer, the professor introduces atoms in optical lattices: standing waves create periodic potentials that can be understood from classical, photon, and microscopic perspectives. Applications include Sisyphus cooling, optical atomic clocks using magic wavelengths, Mott insulator physics in shallow lattices, and pulsed lattices for atom interferometry and measuring the dynamic structure factor. The professor recounts how, in research with Dave Pritchard, pulsing a Bose-Einstein condensate with a standing wave shifted the work from atom interferometry to many-body physics, illustrating the field's combination of precision control with entanglement and many-body physics.

University of Utah scientists have mapped the near-surface geology around Old Faithful in Yellowstone National Park, revealing the heated water reservoir feeding the geyser and how ground shaking behaves between eruptions. The study, published in Geophysical Research Letters with doctoral student Sin-Mei Wu as first author, used a 2015 two-week deployment of 133 low-cost portable seismometers. The Park Service had requested the survey because some nearby buildings sit over thermal features producing excessive heat. Researchers converted ambient vibrations from humans, cars, wind, water, and hydrothermal boilings into seismic signals. They recorded tremors lasting about 60 minutes separated by 30 minutes of quiet, with eruptions occurring at the end of shaking, caused by imploding pressurized bubbles as the reservoir refills. The team identified Old Faithful's hydrothermal reservoir west of the geyser—about 200 meters in diameter, holding roughly 300,000 cubic meters (79 million gallons) of water, compared to about 8,000 gallons released per eruption. Further surveys are planned.

The First Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of Ronald L. Johnson's habeas corpus petition challenging the admission of his confession at a January 1964 Massachusetts trial, where he was convicted of first degree murder, armed robbery, and related offenses for a Boston liquor store holdup in which a police officer was killed. Because the trial concluded before Escobedo and Miranda, the voluntariness standard of Procunier v. Atchley applied. On appeal, Johnson argued that the trial court failed to consider the totality of circumstances, that Lego v. Twomey's preponderance standard should apply retroactively, and that the confession was involuntary as a matter of law. The court found it unnecessary to reach the first two arguments and instead made an independent determination of voluntariness based on undisputed facts: Johnson was injured from a car chase and crash, was interrogated for forty minutes at 5:50 A.M. without Miranda warnings or access to counsel, and participated in suggestive line-ups. Considering his prior experiences with police, his hostile and rights-asserting conduct, the absence of police-inflicted injuries or threats, and the short time between arrest and confession, the court concluded his will was not overborne and the confession was voluntary.

Eighteen researchers, including 13 based in the U.S., have won French President Emmanuel Macron's "Make Our Planet Great Again" climate grants, offering all-expenses-paid research in France. Winners include American Camille Parmesan, a University of Texas scientist studying climate's effects on wildlife, who will work at an ecology station in the Pyrenees, and Benjamin Sanderson, formerly of the National Center for Atmospheric Research in Colorado, who will live in Toulouse. Both cited difficulty obtaining U.S. research funding under Trump.

Secretary Stettinius recommended that governments attend the general conference with open minds and few formal commitments, favoring flexibility since the Dumbarton Oaks proposals had been kept informal to permit modification. Discussions covered the new organization's name, given objections to "United Nations," and the enumeration of principles in Chapter I, including respect for treaties and juridical equality. The term "United Nations" originated on December 31, 1941, when Roosevelt suggested it to Churchill. In January 1945, Stettinius urged informing six Latin American "associated nations" that they could be excluded from the United Nations Conference unless they declared war on the enemies. He had staff prepare memoranda with policy guidance for the President's Big-Three meeting and planned to have conference arrangements, including delegation make-up, date, and place, ready in advance. Voting procedure remained the major unresolved issue; the British would accept a compromise Security Council formula, though the President expected to yield on unanimity while the Russians would yield on their seventeen-vote proposal.

This study describes the Healthy Davis Together (HDT) and Healthy Yolo Together (HYT) community testing program, launched in Davis, California in September 2020 and expanded to Yolo County in July 2021, which provided free saliva-based asymptomatic PCR testing along with education campaigns, protective equipment distribution, and community partnerships. Between November 2020 and June 2022, 770,165 tests were conducted among 89,924 Yolo County residents, reaching approximately 41.1% of the county population and 78.4% of Davis residents. Testing was analyzed across four variant-defined periods (Pre-Delta, Delta, Omicron, Post-Omicron); daily testing peaked during Omicron (895 per 100,000), which also recorded the highest number of positive cases (50.8% of the program's 12,626 positive tests among 11,545 individuals). Highest positivity rates occurred among American Indian/Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander, and Latino participants and those aged 20–44. Women, individuals aged 19–34, and White participants were the most frequent testers; about 18.8% of adult participants tested regularly. New participant enrollment declined over time, and participation dropped after Omicron, possibly due to pandemic fatigue, vaccination, and at-home testing availability. The authors note that behavioral data would be needed to fully explain testing uptake and that such findings can inform future public health strategies.

Worcester city employees collectively earned over $11 million in overtime in 2017, with the police, fire, and public works departments accounting for more than $7 million. Police employees took home $4,399,365 in overtime despite a record-low five homicides, which officials attribute to special projects, training, and events rather than understaffing. Lieutenant John Towns earned the most police overtime at $59,577. Police detail pay totaled $9,326,718, with officer George Kelly earning $100,384 in details, exceeding his $75,508 regular salary. City Manager Edward Augustus Jr. was the city's highest paid employee, and only two of the top 50 earners were women.

This study examined how the everyday act of walking can become an aesthetic experience through art-based practices. Grounded in place-based critical art education and Dewey's concept of aesthetic experience, walking is framed as a bodily, sensory act that shapes and is shaped by place, and as a modest form of bodily resistance distinct from the "tourist gaze" or the flâneur's walk. Over 10 weeks in 2023, seven prospective teachers in an undergraduate fine arts teaching program at a university in western Türkiye participated in the study, which was conducted online after the 2023 earthquake in Türkiye. Using an art-based, interpretive methodology, data were collected through visual diaries, course texts, class recordings, and interviews, and analyzed through axial coding and thematic analysis, with triangulation and participant validation. Participants wrote essays on walking, kept visual diaries, examined Francis Alÿs' performance "The Collector," took photographs, engaged in visual inquiry, and created their own artworks in various media, including videos, performances, collages, and digital works. Findings showed that participants' initially ordinary conceptions of walking expanded to include personal, sensory, and social meanings such as freedom, finding oneself, urbanization, and social problems. They developed sensory awareness, connected walking to art and daily life, and, as prospective teachers, recognized walking's pedagogical value, evaluating it positively as a teaching tool despite difficulties with visualization and public performance. The study concluded that walking-based art education can foster multiple perspectives and help prospective teachers integrate everyday experiences into lesson plans, with future research suggested on participatory and community-based art.

Flu season in Indiana isn't over, with 278 deaths reported so far and the season potentially lasting until mid-April. Infectious diseases like influenza and norovirus can survive on surfaces for a day to weeks, making contact a key transmission route. In a handwashing experiment at IU Health's Pathology Lab, a reporter's hands showed 15 bacteria types, all normal skin flora, with little difference before and after washing, suggesting she should have scrubbed longer. IU Health recommends regular soap, washing 20-30 seconds, scrubbing hands, wrists, and under fingernails, and rinsing thoroughly. A swab of her cell phone found 10 bacteria types, all normal flora. Proper handwashing is the easiest way to prevent disease spread.

India's Supreme Court has ordered that political parties can no longer seek votes in the name of religion, caste, creed, community, or language. The author argues the order is problematic for three reasons. First, it assumes identity-based politics is entirely negative, overlooking that such mobilization arose because discrimination occurred on the same grounds, and that universal franchise helped marginalized groups like Dalits and OBCs organize and gain political power, helping the state reflect society's diversity. Second, while rabid communalism is an unfortunate reality, it persists due to a culture of impunity; the solution lies in stronger implementation of existing laws and democratic self-correction, not judicial fiat, and Hindutva must be fought politically. Third, the order is unimplementable, as identity appeals occur across all elections and the court cannot enforce compliance. The author concludes the judiciary should let electoral democracy evolve on its own.

Apple Inc.'s Form 10-Q for the fiscal quarter ended July 1, 2023 reports total net sales of $81.8 billion, down 1% year-over-year, with net income of $19.9 billion and diluted EPS of $1.26. For the first nine months, net sales were $293.8 billion (down 3%) and net income was $74.0 billion. Q3 Products net sales were $60.6 billion and Services $21.2 billion. By category, iPhone fell 2% to $39.7 billion, Mac fell 7%, iPad fell 20%, and Wearables, Home and Accessories rose 2%, while Services rose 8%. By segment, Americas declined 6%, Europe rose 5%, Greater China rose 8%, Japan fell 11%, and Rest of Asia Pacific fell 8%, with foreign currency weakness unfavorably affecting results. Total assets were $335.0 billion and shareholders' equity $60.3 billion as of July 1, 2023. During the quarter, the Company repurchased $18.0 billion of common stock and paid $3.8 billion in dividends. Commercial paper outstanding was $4.0 billion and term debt $105.3 billion. New products announced included the 15-inch MacBook Air, Mac Studio, Mac Pro, and Apple Vision Pro. In the Epic Games litigation, the Ninth Circuit affirmed the District Court's ruling, and enforcement of the injunction was stayed pending appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court. A European Court of Justice decision on the State Aid Decision is expected in 2024.

Abraaj, the largest private equity firm focused on developing economies with $13.6 billion under management, has been praised by World Bank chief Mr. Kim as a model for private investment in developing markets. Its $1 billion health care fund drew $545 million from investors starting in late 2016 to buy hospitals in Nigeria, Pakistan, and India. In September, investors questioned why over $200 million sat uninvested and requested bank statements, claiming unused money had to be returned within 60 days. Mr. Naqvi cited regulatory delays; unconvinced, investors received over $100 million back in December and demanded an independent auditor, while Abraaj hired KPMG. Investors—including Proparco, CDC Group, the World Bank's IFC, and the Gates Foundation—have sought forensic proof the money wasn't used for Abraaj's own operations. A World Bank corruption review closed without finding wrongdoing. The fund was already struggling; its $145 million CARE hospital investment in India now earns $8 million versus $14 million previously. Mr. Naqvi founded Abraaj in 2002 and is raising a $6 billion fund.

The #MeToo movement prompted rapid political resignations in Canada: Nova Scotia PC leader Jamie Baillie, Ontario PC leader Patrick Brown, and Liberal MP Kent Hehr, following unproven allegations of misconduct. Backlash compared the movement to McCarthyism, raising due process concerns. The author argues parties may hold leaders to higher standards, including against the appearance of impropriety, and that responses to allegations reflect how parties value women. Believing accusers expands rather than upends fairness, presuming truth-telling until evidence weighs otherwise. The timing of revelations is unsurprising now that women are believed, and #MeToo's survival requires fairness while challenging a status quo that has long silenced women.

Indiana is adopting outcomes-based contracting, hiring private tutoring companies to improve middle school reading with pay tied to student results. State education secretary Katie Jenner said no other state offered a successful model to copy, but vendors have pitched solutions since middle school reading scores fell. Contract details, including how much pay will be guaranteed versus incentive-based, remain undecided. The approach, also tried in Texas, Florida, and Arkansas, is promoted by the Center for Outcomes-Based Contracting, which suggests at least 40 percent of contracts depend on defined student gains. Results so far are mixed: about half of 2025 contract goals were met, research is limited, though Stanford researchers called findings from eight districts "promising." Indiana's contracts will target struggling students, who often face attendance and motivation challenges. Jenner is seeking donations and grants and says the state will pay only if partners deliver outcomes.
